property_summary: After calling lockInGuess with a paid 1 ether, the caller's stored guess slot becomes nonzero (block != 0) only when msg.value == 1 ether; i.e., calling lockInGuess with value 1 ether sets guesses[msg.sender].block != 0, whereas allowing zero-value calls would let callers set guess without paying.
Calling lockInGuess must revert unless exactly 1 ether is sent.
lockInGuess only succeeds (does not revert) when the caller sends exactly 1 ether; any other msg.value causes revert.
For any call to lockInGuess, it succeeds (does not revert) iff the caller sends exactly 1 ether.
Calls to lockInGuess succeed (do not revert) exactly when the caller sends 1 ether; any other sent amount causes revert.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess(...) on the correct contract requires sending exactly 1 ether (so a call that sends 0 wei will revert); the mutant that requires msg.value == 0 instead accepts zero-value calls and thus will succeed for some inputs where the reference reverts.

For any caller and any guess hash, the correct contract C requires exactly 1 ether be sent to lockInGuess (so a call with 0 value always reverts), while the mutant accepts 0 value and thus will succeed for some inputs where the reference reverts; the test fuzzes the caller and guess and asserts that lockInGuess with 0 value always reverts on the reference.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess with 0 wei always reverts on the reference contract (it requires exactly 1 ether), but the mutant accepting msg.value == 0 will allow such a call to succeed for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For every caller and guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call that sets a guess, the contract's balance decreases by exactly 1 ether (the contract must be paid 1 ether when a guess is locked); the mutant that accepts msg.value == 0 can produce a scenario where lockInGuess succeeds but the contract balance does not increase by 1 ether, violating this invariant.

For any caller and any guess hash, if lockInGuess succeeds then the caller must have paid exactly 1 ether (so address(c).balance increases by 1 ether); the mutant that accepts msg.value == 0 allows lockInGuess to succeed without payment, breaking this rule for some inputs.

If a caller successfully locks a guess then the contract's balance decreases by exactly 1 ether for that lock-in (i.e., lockInGuess must transfer 1 ether in), so address(c).balance == initial_balance + 0 after failing to lock and == initial_balance + 1 ether after a successful lock.

property_summary: lockInGuess reverts when called without exactly 1 ether (i.e., it only succeeds if called with 1 ether).
Calls to lockInGuess must revert unless exactly 1 ether is sent (so reverted == (amount != 1 ether)).

In the original contract, any caller who already has an active guess (guesses[msg.sender].block != 0) cannot call lockInGuess successfully (it must revert); the mutant can succeed and thus allow a second lock for the same caller.
If lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) then exactly 1 ether was sent with the call.

For any caller and any calldata, the reference contract only accepts lockInGuess when exactly 1 ether is sent (call succeeds); the mutant accepts calls with other ether amounts — so whether lockInGuess call succeeds (does not revert) is equal to (value == 1 ether) for the reference but not for the mutant.

For any caller and any sent value, the original contract reverts (rejects) lockInGuess unless exactly 1 ether is sent; the mutant removes that check so there exist inputs (values ≠ 1 ether) where the mutant accepts the call but the original rejects it.

For any caller and any sent value, the reference contract only accepts lockInGuess when exactly 1 ether is sent (call succeeds) while the mutant accepts calls with other ether amounts; thus the property: lockInGuess(call with value v) succeeds iff v == 1 ether — the mutant breaks this by allowing success for some v != 1 ether.

For any caller and any sent value, the reference contract accepts (call does not revert) lockInGuess(bytes32) if and only if msg.value == 1 ether; the mutant removes that msg.value check so there exist values != 1 ether for which the mutant accepts the call but the reference reverts.

For every caller and every sent value, after a call to lockInGuess(bytes32) on the reference C, the stored guesses[caller].block is nonzero if and only if the call sent exactly 1 ether (the reference only accepts/records guesses when msg.value==1 ether); the mutant can record a guess for some inputs with msg.value != 1 ether, so there exists a fuzzed (caller, value, hash) where the mutant records but the reference does not.

For any caller who pays exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, the stored Guess.block is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was executed in the reference contract (it stores block.number+1), whereas the mutant stores block.number and thus can violate this strict > relation for some inputs.

After a caller successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether, the recorded Guess.block for that caller is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was executed in the correct contract (it stores block.number+1), while the mutant that stores block.number breaks this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).block is strictly greater than the block number at which that call executed in the correct contract (it stores block.number+1); the mutant storing block.number can make the recorded block equal to the call's block, violating the strict > relation for some inputs.

For any caller and any guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call paying exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records a stored block number that is strictly non-equal to the block.number at which settle becomes callable in the same block (i.e. settle cannot succeed in the same block because the stored block is in the future); the mutant that stores block.number can make settle think the guess was set for the current block and thus may allow settle to behave differently (specifically, the stored block equals the current block causing settle's block.number > storedBlock check to fail), which breaks this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess paid with exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses[caller].block in the reference contract is strictly greater than the stored block value that the mutant records when the same call is executed in the same EVM block (i.e., reference stores block.number+1 while mutant stores block.number), so the reference always records a future block number compared with the mutant's stored value for at least one fuzzed caller/block scenario.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess value, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with 1 ether the contract stores exactly the provided hash as the guess for that caller; the mutant stores keccak256(hash) instead and therefore violates this rule for many inputs.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with 1 ether the contract stores guesses(caller).guess equal to the exact provided hash (the mutant stores keccak256(hash) and thus violates this for many hashes).

For any caller and any 32-byte input hash, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether the contract stores a guesses mapping entry whose stored guess, when re-hashed with keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...)), equals keccak256(abi.encodePacked(hash)); the mutant breaks this because it stores keccak256(abi.encodePacked(hash)) directly causing keccak256(abi.encodePacked(stored)) != keccak256(abi.encodePacked(hash)) for many inputs.

For any caller and any 32-byte value x, after calling lockInGuess(x) with exactly 1 ether the stored guess when hashed with keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...)) equals keccak256(abi.encodePacked(x)); the mutant that stores keccak256(x) directly breaks this for many x because keccak256(abi.encodePacked(keccak256(x))) != keccak256(abi.encodePacked(x)).

For any caller and any 32-byte input h, after calling lockInGuess(h) with exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).guess when compared byte-for-byte to h is equal in the correct contract but differs in the mutant which stores keccak256(abi.encodePacked(h)); therefore the property is that reading the public mapping getter returns the exact supplied bytes32 hash, which the mutant will violate for some h.

After a successful lockInGuess call by any account sending exactly 1 ether when they had no active guess, the contract records their guess and nonzero block number; the mutant momentarily clears stored fields before setting them which can cause observable difference when the call reverts during execution (e.g., via a re-entrant fallback) so the invariant that either the call fully succeeds and leaves a nonzero block OR the call reverts never leaving a zeroed guess is broken by the mutant for some reentrant attacker.

For any caller and guess hash, a direct call to lockInGuess that sends exactly 1 ether either fully reverts (leaving no stored guess) or completes leaving a nonzero stored block for that caller; the mutant that zeroes fields mid-call can leave the stored block zero after a seemingly successful call when the caller is a reentrant contract, violating this rule.

For any caller and guess, a call to lockInGuess that completes successfully always results in the caller having a nonzero stored block for their guess; the mutant that zeroes the struct fields before setting them can (for some reentrant caller) leave the stored block zero even though the call returned, violating this invariant.

For any caller and guess hash, a completed call to lockInGuess that returns successfully always results in the caller having a nonzero stored block in the contract (i.e., their guess is recorded); the mutant that zeroes the struct fields before setting them can, for some reentrant caller, return successfully while leaving the stored block zero, violating this rule.

For any caller and guess hash, if lockInGuess returns successfully then the stored guesses(caller).block is nonzero; the mutant that zeroes the struct fields before setting them can (for some re-entrant caller) return successfully while leaving the stored block zero, violating this rule.

For any caller who previously locked a guess for block N, the correct contract rejects settling in block N (requires current block > N), whereas the mutant (>=) allows settling in block N — enabling access to blockhash of the same block and thus changing observable behavior (e.g., success of settle in that block).

For any caller who previously locked a guess matching the blockhash-based answer, calling settle returns the 2 ether prize (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether); the mutant zeroes the stored guess before computing the answer and therefore can never pay out even when the original would, breaking this property for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully locked a guess equal to the keccak256(blockhash(lockedBlock)) the correct contract will pay out (reducing address(c).balance by 2 ether) when settle() is called after that block; the mutant zeros the stored guess before computing the answer and therefore never pays out for at least some valid locked guesses.

For any caller who previously locked a guess, calling settle after the locked block causes the reference contract to possibly pay out (reducing address(c).balance) when the stored guess equals the block-derived answer; the mutant clears the stored guess before computing the answer and therefore for some locked guesses the mutant will not pay out while the reference would.

If a caller locked a guess and then settle() is called after the locked block, the reference contract will transfer 2 ether to the caller exactly when the stored guess equals keccak256(blockhash(lockedBlock)); the mutant clears the stored guess before computing the answer and therefore for some locked guesses the reference pays out (c.balance decreases by 2 ether) while the mutant does not.

If a user locks a guess and the chain advances past the locked block, the correct contract will compare the stored guess against keccak256(blockhash(lockedBlock)) (so the stored guess value is used in the comparison); the mutant clears the stored guess before computing the answer so there exist locked guesses for which the correct contract would pay out (reducing address(c).balance) but the mutant never does.

For any caller who locked a nonzero guess and the correct timing, calling settle never pays out unless their stored guess equals the blockhash-derived answer; the mutant instead pays whenever the stored guess is zero, so there exist inputs (a caller who stored bytes32(0)) that cause a payout in the mutant but not in the reference.

For any caller who locks a nonzero-guess deposit and later calls settle after the required block, the reference C never pays out unless the stored guess equals the blockhash-derived answer; the mutant instead may pay out whenever the stored guess equals bytes32(0), violating the rule (there exist inputs where guess==bytes32(0) causing payout in mutant but not in reference).

For any caller who locked a 1 ether guess and later calls settle after the required block, the reference contract never increases address(c).balance (i.e., does not pay out) unless the stored guess equals the blockhash-derived answer; the mutant instead may pay out when the stored guess is bytes32(0), so there exist fuzzed inputs (a caller who locked bytes32(0)) that make the mutant increase address(c).balance but the reference does not.

Reference: settle never transfers out 2 ether unless the stored guess equals the keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)); Mutant: settle instead transfers whenever the stored guess equals bytes32(0), so there exist inputs where the mutant pays out but the reference does not.

For any caller who locked a guess and waited past the target block, the reference contract only pays out (reduces its balance) when the stored guess equals the keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)); the mutant instead pays out when the stored guess equals bytes32(0), so there exist fuzzed inputs (a caller who locked bytes32(0)) that make the mutant transfer 2 ether while the reference does not.

After a successful settle call that may pay out, the reference contract always clears the stored guess slot (guesses[msg.sender].block == 0) while the mutant that omits clearing can leave guesses[msg.sender].block nonzero (allowing repeated settles); the test fuzzes caller and blockNumber offset to trigger a winning settle and then asserts the stored block is zero.

After any call to settle that may succeed or fail for a caller, the reference contract always clears the stored guess.block for that caller (making guesses[msg].block == 0), whereas the mutant that omits clearing can leave guesses[msg].block nonzero for some input, so a second settle call may observe a nonzero stored block when the reference always has zero.
